tier_reason: docs/DESIGN.md (Performance section) gives one first-party prose figure, scanning 'around twice as fast then scanf', and points to the CI benchmark run; the benchmark code is public (test/benchmark/bench_scan.cpp, Catch2 BENCHMARK vs sscanf) but no compiler, flags or CPU are tied to the figure and no results are committed, so it cannot reach A or B.

corrections.caveats: Single first-party prose sentence in docs/DESIGN.md ('Scanning on the other hand is around twice as fast then scanf'); no result table, compiler, flags or CPU are given and no benchmark output is committed. The DESIGN.md points to 'the benchmark tests inside the CI': the CI matrix (GCC 11-13, Clang 16-19 on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners) runs ctest --verbose in both Debug and Release builds, so it is unknown which build or compiler the 2x figure came from, and the CI logs could not be opened here. In test/benchmark/bench_scan.cpp the sscanf cases are mislabelled 'snprintf'; the four cases are a 445-character literal-only format, a single-digit int, a 19-digit int64 and a 16-digit hex uint64, each with a compile-time and a runtime format string, and the claim does not say whether the runtime-format path (parsed sequentially, which DESIGN.md calls a performance overhead) is also 2x. The sscanf baseline is the C library (glibc on the CI runners), not a C++ standard library. Its own DESIGN.md says formatting is about 1.5-2x slower than fmtlib and similar to printf, so the speed win is scanning only; the headline win is binary size (about 5 kB vs 191 kB for fmt, 38x smaller). No independent measurement was found (one web search).

notes: Real entry, record accurate; keep at tier C. Shortcomings: prose-only 2x claim with no stated compiler/flags/CPU, CI benchmark output not committed and run in both Debug and Release, sscanf rows mislabelled 'snprintf' in bench_scan.cpp, formatting is slower than fmt. Metadata checked: MIT, 189 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-08-26 (active), Conan Center badge in README.

tier_reason: The author's own performance page reports times relative to FastFormat.Format for seven scenarios against a column labelled 'Streams (snprintf())', IOStreams, Boost.Format and Loki.SafeFormat, with compilers named (GCC 4.1/4.2, Visual C++ 6/9) and public benchmark code (test/performance/ in the repo, 'make test.performance' in the 0.2.1 beta 6 distribution), but no optimisation flags and no CPU model; first-party with partial methodology is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Times relative to FastFormat.Format (above 1.0 means FastFormat.Format faster), averaged over five platform/compiler rows, scenarios 1-7: 'Streams (snprintf())' 1.49, 0.83, 1.15, 0.66, 1.63, 6.87, 1.64; IOStreams 3.28, 2.16, 5.08, 2.41, 2.82, 9.96, 2.86; Boost.Format 10.29, 5.18, 12.10, 5.57, 8.68, 17.27, 8.94; Loki.SafeFormat 2.28, 1.36, 2.03, 1.35, 2.17, 5.47, 2.16; FastFormat.Write 0.74, 0.84, 0.61, 0.81, 0.70, 0.88, 0.71. Page summary: faster than Streams by 15-580% except scenarios 2 and 4 (17% and 34% slower); faster than IOStreams by ~100-900% in all cases; faster than Boost.Format by ~400-1650%; FastFormat.Write is ~25% faster than FastFormat.Format and faster than all competitors except in scenarios 2 and 4. Headline: 5-17 times faster than Boost.Format, 1.5-5.5 times faster than Loki.SafeFormat.
corrections.workload: Seven scenarios from the FastFormat 0.2.1 beta 6 test/performance programs, each formatting into a std::string per iteration with functional equivalents for the other libraries: (1) 'My name is {0} {1}; I am {2} years old; call me {0}' (cvu.ex.1); (2) name, int age, float height for five records (name_age_height); (3) one int from INT_MIN to INT_MAX (one_integer); (4) one pointer (one_pointer); (5) three strings with repeats (scenario1); (6) ten strings, including a 1000-char one, formatted twice (ten_strings_twice); (7) three strings and one int (three_strings_one_integer). Run on Ubuntu x86 (GCC 4.2), Ubuntu x64 (GCC 4.1), Windows x86 (Visual C++ 6 and 9) and Windows x64 (Visual C++ 9); timed with the STLSoft platformstl performance_counter.
corrections.caveats: Author's own page from the 2008-2009 era (FastFormat 0.2.1 beta 6; GCC 4.1/4.2, Visual C++ 6/9); no CPU, RAM, optimisation flags or date are given. The printf-family win comes from the MSVC CRT rows: on the two Ubuntu/GCC rows glibc snprintf beat FastFormat.Format in 11 of 14 cells (FastFormat.Format won only scenario 6 on both and scenario 3 on x86; derived from page data), and the page itself reports FastFormat.Format 17% and 34% slower than snprintf on average in scenarios 2 and 4. FastFormat.Write beat glibc snprintf in 10 of 14 GCC cells, losing scenarios 2 and 4 (derived from page data). The averages mix platforms and compilers. The current repo's harness (test/performance/*, updated February 2024) times ::sprintf into a 10001-char stack buffer followed by a std::string construction, while the page labels the column snprintf(). The IOStreams column is the C++ standard library (libstdc++ of GCC 4.1/4.2 and the Visual C++ 6/9 library), so the C++ comparison is direct but on toolchains that are 15+ years old. The ACCU Overload 91 article (June 2009) could not be opened (egress blocked); a web search snippet reports about 3x faster than printf-family, 6x faster than IOStreams and 17x faster than Boost.Format. Requires the header-only STLSoft 1.9.121+ library. The only commit since February 2024 is 'Boilerplate (#4)' (2026-08-04), so 'active' reflects project scaffolding, not new performance work.

notes: Numbers in the record match the page exactly (the column is labelled 'Streams (snprintf())'); keep at tier C. Shortcomings to record: no CPU or flags, 2008-era compilers, win over snprintf holds mainly against the MSVC CRT (glibc snprintf faster in 11 of 14 GCC cells, derived from page data), slower than snprintf in scenarios 2 and 4.
